body:
Tangaliya: raised dots created on the loom

Tangaliya is a traditional weaving craft associated with Surendranagar district, particularly the Wadhwan region and neighbouring weaving settlements. The craft has a strong association with Dangasia or Dangashiya weavers.

Its most recognisable feature is a surface of tiny raised dots, called daana, arranged into geometric patterns. These dots are created by incorporating additional yarn during weaving. They are not beads sewn onto the finished textile.

Tangaliya textiles have historically been associated with garments and shawls used by pastoral communities, including the Bharwad. This distinction between makers and users is important: Dangasia refers to the traditional weaving community, whereas Bharwad identifies an important community for whom such textiles were produced and worn.

The registered GI is Tangaliya Shawl, application number 127. Its registration certificate is dated 4 September 2009.

Tangaliya is woven decoration, not embroidery. A raised dotted appearance does not by itself establish that a textile has been embroidered.

Embroidery in Kutch: decoration added with stitches

Embroidery uses a needle and thread to create designs on an existing fabric. Kutch is known for numerous community-specific embroidery traditions, often incorporating coloured threads, geometric or floral patterns and small mirrors.

Embroidery has traditionally been practised by women and has served several purposes: decorating garments, preparing marriage textiles, furnishing homes and expressing social or community identity. Different groups developed recognisable preferences in colours, motifs, stitches and overall composition.

Banni embroidery

Banni refers to the grassland region of Kutch district. It is not a separate administrative district and does not represent a single caste or artisan community.

Embroidery associated with the Banni region includes work produced by communities such as the Jat, Mutwa and Meghwal. These traditions have their own visual characteristics. For example, some Banni-region embroidery is recognised for dense, carefully arranged stitching and mirror decoration, while the exact style depends on the community and type of work.

For a matching question, therefore, the reliable geographical association is Banni region, Kutch district. It would be inaccurate to assign every Banni embroidery tradition exclusively to one community.

Rabari embroidery

The Rabari are traditionally pastoral communities found in Kutch and other parts of Gujarat, including Saurashtra. Rabari women have developed distinctive embroidery practices for garments and household textiles.

Rabari embroidery is commonly associated with bold forms, geometric and animal-inspired motifs, contrasting coloured threads and mirror work. These features reflect a living community tradition; they are not an exclusive test that can identify every Rabari textile without considering its other characteristics.

Ahir embroidery

Ahir embroidery is another important Kutch tradition associated with Ahir women. It is recognised for colourful threadwork, often featuring curved lines, floral forms and mirrors.

The precise motifs and stitches can vary among artisans and localities. The basic distinction remains that Ahir identifies a community-linked embroidery tradition, whereas Banni primarily identifies a region containing several embroidery traditions.

How to distinguish weaving and embroidery

TraditionTraditional associationPlaceIdentifying feature
TangaliyaDangasia weaversSurendranagarRaised dots woven into cloth
Banni embroideryJat, Mutwa, Meghwal and other groupsBanni, KutchCommunity-specific stitched patterns
Rabari embroideryRabari womenKutch and wider GujaratBold motifs and mirror work
Ahir embroideryAhir womenKutchCurving motifs, colourful stitching and mirrors

Geographical Indication status of Kutch embroidery

Kutch Embroidery is a registered GI, application number 103, with a certificate dated 10 July 2008. It is the broad registered GI name relevant to traditional embroidery from Kutch.

The terms Banni embroidery, Rabari embroidery and Ahir embroidery identify regional or community traditions. They should not automatically be treated as 3 independently registered GI names. Equally, Rabari embroidery made elsewhere in Gujarat should not automatically be assumed to fall within the registered specifications of Kutch Embroidery.

Prelims focus

  • Tangaliya: Dangasia weavers, Surendranagar district, raised woven dots.
  • Bharwad: an important traditional user community for Tangaliya textiles.
  • Banni: grassland region within Kutch district.
  • Rabari embroidery: community-linked tradition associated with pastoral Rabari groups.
  • Ahir embroidery: colourful stitched and often mirrored textiles associated with Ahir women.
  • Kutch Embroidery GI registration certificate: 2008.
  • Trap: Banni is a geographical region; Ahir and Rabari are community identities.

[Sources: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Chapter 1, Crafts Heritage, printed pp. 9–12; GCERT, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 2, section on embroidery, including Banni and Jat traditions; Gujarat Tourism, Tangaliya craft page and Living and Learning Design Centre Crafts Museum page, consulted 23 November 2026; Khamir, Embroidery, craft documentation, consulted 23 November 2026; Intellectual Property India, GI Registry application records 127 and 103, consulted 23 November 2026.]

title: Tangaliya Weaving and the Embroidery Traditions of Banni, Rabari and Ahir Communities

body:
Sankheda: painted and lacquered wooden furniture

Sankheda furniture is a traditional woodcraft associated with the town of Sankheda in Chhota Udepur district. Its makers are particularly associated with the Kharadi artisan community, along with traditional Suthar woodworkers.

The craft is known for wooden furniture shaped into smooth, rounded parts and decorated with painted designs and lacquer. Traditional products include cradles, swings, chairs, stools and tables. Floral and abstract decorative patterns, often combined with bright colours and metallic-looking highlights, give the furniture a distinctive appearance.

The method is different from textile painting. The decorative surface is created on a wooden object that has been shaped for use as furniture. Lacquer provides a characteristic finished appearance.

The district-name distinction

Older references may associate Sankheda with Vadodara district. However, under Gujarat's present district arrangement, Sankheda is in Chhota Udepur district, which was formed in 2013. Therefore, a question about its current district should be answered using Chhota Udepur, while older references may retain Vadodara.

Sankheda Furniture is registered as a GI under application number 100. Its registration certificate is dated 10 July 2008.

Saurashtra Moti Bharatkam: decorative beadwork

Moti Bharatkam is a Gujarati term for decorative beadwork. In this craft, small beads, particularly coloured glass beads, are joined with thread or attached to a supporting surface to form decorative patterns.

The craft is closely associated with Saurashtra, including areas such as Bhavnagar, Rajkot, Amreli and Junagadh. It has traditionally been practised by women belonging to several communities, including Kathi, Kanbi, Ahir and other regional groups. No single community should be treated as the exclusive practitioner of all Saurashtra beadwork.

Traditional beadwork can be used to make torans for decorating entrances, hanging ornaments, household decorations, ceremonial objects and decorative items associated with marriage customs or domestic life. Beaded decorations may also be made for animals.

A toran is a decorative hanging generally placed across an entrance or doorway. In beadwork, its design is formed from arranged beads rather than printed or painted patterns.

Saurashtra Moti Bharatkam (Bead Work) of Gujarat is listed as a registered GI in the official 31 October 2026 register. Its application number is 1280, and its registration certificate document is dated 28 March 2026. The registered applicant is Motikaam Hastkala Vikas Trust, Bhavnagar.

Comparing the crafts

AttributeSankheda furnitureSaurashtra Moti Bharatkam
Main materialWoodBeads and thread
MethodWood shaping, painting and lacqueringJoining or attaching beads
Principal geographical associationSankheda, Chhota UdepurSaurashtra, including Bhavnagar
Traditional makersKharadi and Suthar woodworkersWomen from several Saurashtra communities
GI registration year20082026

What the comparison teaches

A decorative design does not by itself determine the category of a handicraft. A painted wooden cradle remains a woodcraft. A toran made by joining glass beads is beadwork. In contrast, a textile design made by stitching coloured thread is embroidery.

The most reliable approach is to identify the object, its material and the craft process together before matching it with a geographical centre or artisan community.

Prelims focus

  • Sankheda furniture: Kharadi artisans, woodcraft, Chhota Udepur district.
  • Older sources may place Sankheda in Vadodara district.
  • Sankheda Furniture GI registration certificate: 2008.
  • Moti Bharatkam: decorative beadwork associated with Saurashtra.
  • Bhavnagar is an important association for Saurashtra Moti Bharatkam.
  • Saurashtra Moti Bharatkam GI registration certificate document: 2026.
  • Trap: Beadwork is not the same as raised-dot Tangaliya weaving.

[Sources: GCERT, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 2, sections on beadwork and woodcraft; Development Commissioner (Handicrafts), A Compendium of Indian Handicrafts and Handlooms Covered under Geographical Indications, entry Sankheda Furniture, p. 132; Gujarat Tourism, Sankheda Furniture, Chhota Udepur destination page, consulted 23 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, handicrafts publication, section on embroidery, appliqué and beadwork in Saurashtra, consulted 23 November 2026; Intellectual Property India, GI Registry application records 100 and 1280 and registered-GI list as on 31 October 2026, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A Sankheda wooden cradle with painted lacquer decoration beside a Saurashtra toran made of coloured beads joined with thread.
pictures.caption: A lacquered wooden cradle and a beadwork toran are distinguished by their materials and uses.

title: Sankheda Furniture and Saurashtra Beadwork: Two Non-Printing Craft Traditions

body:
Meaning and purpose

Mata-ni-Pachedi is a traditional form of painted and printed ritual cloth associated particularly with Ahmedabad, Gujarat. The name is commonly understood as referring to a cloth placed behind or in honour of the Mother Goddess.

Unlike textiles made principally for clothing, Mata-ni-Pachedi has an important ritual and devotional function. Traditionally, such cloths helped create a sacred space for worship, including in circumstances where a permanent temple structure was unavailable.

Thus, the cultural identity of this craft depends not only on its decorative appearance but also on the social and ritual purpose of the finished cloth.

The Devipujak and Chitara connection

The tradition is closely associated with the Devipujak community, historically also referred to as Vaghri. Skilled Chitara painter families have played an important role in producing these ritual textiles.

In a matching question, the association Mata-ni-Pachedi — Devipujak or Vaghri — Ahmedabad is especially important. However, the reference to Chitara artisans concerns the painting tradition and should not be confused with the name of the ritual cloth itself.

Distinctive visual features

Traditional Mata-ni-Pachedi compositions commonly feature a central representation of a Mother Goddess, accompanied by smaller figures, animals, attendants, narrative scenes or decorative borders. The compositions frequently use a distinctive arrangement of red, black and white.

Both painting and block-printing methods have been associated with this textile tradition. The essential point for preliminary examinations is that Mata-ni-Pachedi is a ritual painted or printed cloth tradition, rather than a woven dotted textile such as Tangaliya or a silk ikat such as Patola.

Its cultural meaning is also different from the primarily ornamental function of ordinary decorative block-printed textiles. Mata-ni-Pachedi combines visual art, craft skill and devotional practice.

Geographical Indication status

Mata ni Pachedi is registered as a GI under application number 694. Its application was filed on 14 July 2020, but the registration certificate was issued on 31 March 2023.

This is a useful example of why the filing year and registration year must be kept separate. The application date does not establish that GI registration had already been granted in 2020.

Distinction from Rogan and Ajrakh

CraftMain identityKey association
Mata-ni-PachediRitual painted or printed clothDevipujak and Chitara; Ahmedabad
RoganOil-based textile paintingKhatri artisans; Nirona, Kutch
AjrakhPatterned textile block printingKhatri printers; Ajrakhpur and Dhamadka, Kutch

All 3 traditions decorate cloth, but their methods and cultural settings distinguish them. In particular, the ritual role and Devipujak association of Mata-ni-Pachedi should not be replaced by the Khatri and Kutch associations of Rogan or Ajrakh.

Prelims focus

  • Mata-ni-Pachedi: ritual painted or printed cloth associated with Mother Goddess worship.
  • Traditional community: Devipujak, historically also called Vaghri.
  • Traditional painter association: Chitara families.
  • Principal geographical association: Ahmedabad.
  • Characteristic colours: red, black and white.
  • GI application: 2020; GI registration certificate: 2023.
  • Trap: Mata-ni-Pachedi is not the Rogan painting tradition of Nirona.

[Sources: Ahmedabad University, Kala Katha: A Sacred Story on Cloth, event documentation on the Devipujak and Chitara tradition, consulted 23 November 2026; Sahapedia, Kalamkari of Gujarat: Mata ni Pachhedi, sections on community, ritual use and textile imagery, consulted 23 November 2026; Intellectual Property India, GI Registry application record 694, including filing date and certificate date, consulted 23 November 2026.]
